references.text: Job says that God does not reject the innocent and does not support the wicked – a challenge to the same assumption Jesus rejects here, namely that suffering is always a direct result of personal sin ([ref:Job 8:20|Job 8:20]).
Job asks how a person can be righteous before God, and acknowledges that there is no simple connection between suffering and guilt ([ref:Job 9:2-3|Job 9:2-3]).

The disciples ask Jesus whether the man born blind sinned himself or if his parents sinned, and Jesus rejects the idea that blindness was caused by anyone's personal sin – a direct parallel to the rejection of the link between suffering and sin in Luke 13:2 ([ref:Joh 9:2-3|John 9:2-3]).
Job points out that the wicked often live long lives and prosper, undermining the notion that misfortune always strikes sinners more than others ([ref:Job 21:7-9|Job 21:7-9]).

Ecclesiastes reflects on how both the righteous and the wicked meet the same fate – what happens to one happens to all – and thus one cannot infer guilt from suffering ([ref:Fork 9:1-2|Ecclesiastes 9:1-2]).

Ecclesiastes observes that there are righteous people who perish despite their righteousness, and wicked people who live long despite their evil – a challenge to simple retribution thinking ([ref:Fork 7:15|Ecclesiastes 7:15]).

Jesus follows up with another example – the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell – and repeats that they were no more guilty than others, but urges everyone to repent ([ref:Luk 13:4-5|Luke 13:4-5]).
Paul states that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, supporting Jesus' point that everyone needs repentance, not only those struck by visible misfortunes ([ref:Rom 3:23|Romans 3:23]).

The Lord declares through Ezekiel that he judges each person according to their own ways and calls for repentance – God's justice is individual, not collectively punitive based on external events ([ref:Esek 18:29-30|Ezekiel 18:29-30]).
